15.13 states the rule, that the finally disposes of the resource and only a null resource skips Dispose (PDF p. 215 lines 8-10), and its 'precisely equivalent' code (lines 11-22) cannot be literal for every resource the clause admits: for a plain disposable struct, which 15.13 expressly allows (PDF p. 214 lines 45-46, PDF p. 215 lines 1-4), r1 != null is a compile-time error (PDF p. 181 lines 23-26), and for a class with a user-defined != the literal code would skip a non-null resource against lines 8-10. On this reading the observable behavior matches the 7th edition and csc (BODY:1:0), and the one remaining difference, the 7th edition's ban on boxing a value resource (PDF p. 362), cannot be observed because nothing reads the resource after Dispose.

The multiple-resource text (PDF p. 215 lines 23-49) only repeats the single-resource finally for each resource, so the same whole-text reading applies (PDF p. 215 lines 8-10, PDF p. 181 lines 23-26) and it shares -015's semantics and any test; the retained facets (nested equivalence, acquisition order, reverse disposal) match the 7th edition 13.14. The residual no-boxing difference is unobservable, as for -015.

A program whose only unreachable statement is a throw statement after a return (likewise an empty block {} or an empty statement ;) compiles at ISO-1 with at least one warning (csc reports none, a recorded departure); a block holding other statements is not a clean test, since those statements warn in both editions.

foreach (string s in new int[] {...}) compiles at ISO-1 and throws System.InvalidCastException at the first element, as the IEnumerable-view control does (CAST:0); csc rejects it with CS0030, a recorded departure.

foreach (long x in new int[] {...}) compiles at ISO-1 and throws System.InvalidCastException at the first element (csc prints SUM:26, a recorded departure); the same loop with an int iteration variable succeeds.
